title: The Four Loves
author: C.S. Lewis
edition_analyzed: Original US and UK editions (1960); content is consistent across standard editions.
target_audience: Adults seeking to understand the nature of love
Students of Christian theology and philosophy
Readers interested in moral and relational exploration
core_themes: The nature and varieties of love
The distinction between natural and divine love
The dangers and rewards of loving deeply
The relationship between human love and God's love
primary_purpose: To examine and categorize the four main types of love described in both Greek and Christian traditions—affection, friendship, eros, and charity—exploring their virtues, pitfalls, and place in human and spiritual life.

structure_format.narrative_style: Analytical, philosophical, conversational, and sometimes anecdotal
structure_format.organization: Divided into an introduction and four primary sections, each focused on a specific type of love (Storge, Philia, Eros, Agape)
features: Rooted in Christian and classical references
Blends personal reflection with scholarly analysis
Rich use of metaphors and literary illustrations

key_concepts_lessons: Storge (affection) is the most humble and widely diffused of loves, representing fondness through familiarity.
Philia (friendship) is the least celebrated and most rational of loves, built on shared values and companionship.
Eros (romantic love) transcends mere lust and finds its fulfillment in loving the beloved as themselves.
Agape (charity) is the highest form of love, self-giving and unconditional, reflective of divine love.
All natural loves can become either glorious or destructive depending on whether they are subordinated to or separated from the love of God.
Human loves are limited and flawed without the transformative grace of charity.
notable_features: Based on Lewis’s radio talks for the BBC
Anchors concepts in both lived experience and Scripture
Draws on Greek terminology to categorize types of love
Insights into both secular and Christian views on relationships
cultural_historical_context: Written and published in post-World War II Britain by one of the twentieth century’s preeminent Christian thinkers, The Four Loves reflects the era’s resurgence in religious reflection and interest in the nature of meaningful human relationships.
reception_impact: Considered a classic in Christian literature and popular philosophy
Praised for its accessible treatment of complex relational questions
Frequently referenced in discussions on love and ethics
Sometimes critiqued for reflecting Lewis’s personal and historical biases
comparable_titles: The Art of Loving by Erich Fromm
Love and Responsibility by Karol Wojtyła (Pope John Paul II)
